description: The Barnes-Hut algorithm recursively subdivides space into a quadtree (2D) or octree (3D), grouping distant particles into single center-of-mass nodes. This reduces gravitational force calculation from O(N^2) to O(N log N) by approximating far-field interactions. The key parameter theta controls the accuracy-speed tradeoff: smaller theta means more accurate but slower computation.
mathematical_formalization: For each particle i, traverse the tree. For node with center-of-mass C, total mass M, and size s at distance d: if s/d < theta, approximate F_i += G * m_i * M * (C - r_i) / |C - r_i|^3. Otherwise, recurse into children. Complexity: O(N log N) vs O(N^2) for direct summation.
analogical_connections: KD-trees in machine learning for nearest-neighbor search use identical spatial subdivision logic
DNS hierarchical caching groups requests by domain proximity, analogous to grouping particles by spatial proximity
Image compression quadtrees recursively subdivide pixel regions by similarity, paralleling mass aggregation
implementation_hypothesis: Build an octree each timestep: insert particles, compute center-of-mass bottom-up, then walk tree per particle with theta=0.5. For a minimal sim, a 2D quadtree suffices. Each node stores: bounds, total_mass, center_of_mass, children[4]. Force walk is a recursive descent with the s/d < theta pruning criterion.
experiment_seed: Compare wall-clock time and energy drift between direct O(N^2) summation and Barnes-Hut at theta={0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0} for N={1000, 10000, 100000}. Plot accuracy (energy conservation) vs speedup.
